Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska on Tuesday, completing a political comeback in a state Donald Trump has repeatedly won by wide margins. Her victory gives Democrats a 56-44 Senate majority, marking their biggest net gain in Senate seats since 1958.
Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, overcoming allegations that members of her campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares the incumbent’s name and completing a political comeback in a state President Donald Trump repeatedly won by wide margins.
The Alaska race is the last US Senate contest to be resolved in this year's midterm elections , and Peltola’s victory expands the Democrats’ majority after they retook control of the chamber. The party already won campaigns in conservative states including South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and, most recently, Mississippi.
With Peltola’s victory, Democrats flipped nine Senate seats, the most since 1958. Republicans entered the midterms with a 53-47 majority, while Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin.
Messages seeking comment were left with both campaigns Tuesday night.
Read more 'Climate action is alive': Triumphant Democrats attend COP31 summit shunned by Trump
Peltola, in a statement on social media, said there “is no greater honour than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first. Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work.”
Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, after former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans , including one endorsed by Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the US House race, where independent candidate Bill Hill is challenging Republican Rep. Nick Begich.
Peltola previously held the state's lone House seat, making her the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress. She lost her bid for a second full term to Begich in 2024, but she became central to Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate in 2026.
In the campaign’s final stretch, however, she faced allegations that her team helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run in order to siphon votes from the incumbent.
Read more Democrat Scott Colom wins historic Senate race in Mississippi
Trump called for Peltola’s prosecution after The New York Times first reported the allegation less than a week before the November 3 election. Peltola denied any involvement.
“I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau days before the election.
Dan J. Sullivan has denied any contact with Peltola’s campaign or running at the Democrats' behest. He has not responded to messages from The Associated Press since The Times’ article was published.
The Times report was based partly on text messages and other documents and interviews with Peltola’s former campaign manager, who was fired shortly before this year’s open primary and later sought to recant her statements. But the second Sullivan had already been on Trump’s mind. He referred to him multiple times during a rally in support of the senator in mid-October.
Later, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit that Trump said he ordered. It sought to block certification of the race if the incumbent were to lose, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. Peltola called the lawsuit “flagrant corruption”.

The case was dismissed by a federal judge, but the Justice Department appealed. Attorneys for the state sought dismissal, saying officials should be able to conduct the election “without unwarranted interference by the United States .” They also argued the ballot was designed to distinguish the two Sullivans as much as possible and that Alaska’s ranked choice voting process would allow any voters who might be confused to rank them.
The Justice Department also confirmed the existence of a criminal investigation, but Alaska’s US attorney would not say what potential crimes authorities were looking into.
Peltola finished first in the primary with 49.5% of the vote, followed by the incumbent with 41.4%.
Dan J. Sullivan finished a distant third with about 2.5%, but he advanced to the general election as one of the top four finishers. He was listed on both ballots as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent.
During the campaign, Peltola tapped into Alaskans’ frustrations with high fuel prices and other costs. Those concerns hit especially hard in remote communities that rely on diesel for electricity and heat and are often only accessible by air or water.
Her campaign peppered social media with photos of her travels around the state as she sought to separate herself from national Democrats and build a coalition of support around a platform of “Alaska first”.
“Alaskans who know me know that I’m not liberal or radical,” Peltola said. “I am only interested in working for Alaska and working for the best interest of Alaskans, in as nonpartisan of a way as I possibly can.”
The race attracted a flood of spending by outside groups and at times turned negative, with the campaigns accusing each other of spreading lies. Trump and Vice President JD Vance made separate trips to the state in the month before the election in support of the incumbent.
“Lower 48” became something of an insult bandied by both sides. Sullivan and his supporters tried to align Peltola with “Lower 48 liberals” who want to restrict oil and gas drilling, mining and other resource development in the state. Peltola said that while she would work with Trump to get things done for Alaska, “I will never put any Lower 48 politician before Alaskans. That’s the difference between Dan and me.”
When Sullivan took issue with Peltola reading off note cards during a debate – “You can’t cue-card your way to the Senate,” he told reporters – Peltola said she simply was prepared. She also pushed back against Sullivan’s assertion that she was ineffective during her time in the House, saying she worked well with him as part of the state’s three-person delegation in Washington.
Peltola postponed two days of campaign events in late October after her campaign said she suffered minor injuries in a car accident in Anchorage.
Peltola, who is Yup’ik, emphasised her Alaska roots and resurrected the “fish, family and freedom” tagline from her prior campaigns. She spoke about growing up in western Alaska and fishing for salmon on the Kuskokwim River with her father and spending parts of the summer at fish camp with her children and late husband, who died in September 2023.
She said the fish and wildlife that Alaskans long relied on to fill their freezers for the winter were becoming harder to find. The changes were forcing people to buy more food and other staples at the store – supplies that must be barged or flown in – and deal with “crushing prices,” she said.
Peltola also said she saw members of Congress who were “more focused on their stock portfolios” than helping ease those costs and vowed to push back against the billionaire class.
Peltola will be just the fifth Democrat since statehood to represent Alaska in the Senate. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014.

Illegal activities in the Amazon pose grave risks to uncontacted Indigenous groups like Brazil’s Awa, advocates stress.
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

The Israeli parliament on Tuesday elected as new speaker an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Matan Kahana, a former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu.
The Israeli parliament, or Knesset , elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.
Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.
The parliament speaker is an important office given that it sets the timetable for parliamentary business and can therefore speed up or delay debates or votes on proposed legislation.
Read more Eisenkot pushes October 7 inquiry as Netanyahu targets Arab parties in tense new parliament
Kahana, a 54-year-old former special forces soldier, is expected as soon as Wednesday to start the process of undoing much of the agenda of Netanyahu, Israel 's longest serving prime minister who has been in and out of office for three decades.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a majority in the 120-member Knesset in October 27 elections , with the two blocs trading barbs since then.
The vote for parliament speaker crystallised their standoff, with a heated debate before the vote.
In October, Eisenkot's wide-ranging bloc secured 48 seats, while Netanyahu's finished with 53. Two Arab-majority slates won an unprecedented 19 seats on the back of anger over Netanyahu's hard-right government.
On Tuesday, the two lists voted for Eisenkot's candidate Kahana as parliament speaker, with one Arab Knesset member absent.
"I will be a Knesset speaker for everyone, irrespective of race, religion or gender," said Kahana during his inauguration speech immediately after the vote.
Netanyahu's and Eisenkot's parties met Sunday on the possibility of joining a unity government but the meeting appeared to be largely a formality, with both men saying they should be prime minister.
Netanyahu, who has reportedly been urging US President Donald Trump to resume war on Iran , has talked up the threat from Tehran as he insists on the need for a unity government.
Eisenkot said afterwards that Netanyahu was unfit to "remain at the helm of government for even one more minute" after an explosive media report that his allies tried to make up allegations of fraud to frame lawmakers from the Arab minority.
On Tuesday, Israel's central elections committee released a statement regarding the ongoing investigation into the fraud accusations led by the Shin Bet intelligence agency.
"At this stage, there is no evidence that bribes were paid to voters on a scale that could have affected the election results," it said.
With Kahana at the helm and if Eisenkot retains the backing of the Arab-Israeli parties, he has an opportunity to deal serious blows to Netanyahu's legislative agenda even before a possible government is formed.
Eisenkot has said he wants to rescind sweeping reforms to reduce the independence of the judiciary that were advanced by Netanyahu, who has been enraged over corruption charges against him that could land him in prison if he loses power.
The judicial reforms initiated shortly after Netanyahu began his latest term in December 2022 triggered some of Israel's largest ever protests, bringing tens of thousands to the streets, with liberals fearing an erosion of the country's democracy.
Eisenkot has also vowed to quickly set up a state commission of inquiry to investigate security failures that led to Hamas 's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu, who has built his brand on saying he will ensure Israel's security, has refused an independent probe, instead proposing one whose members would be chosen by politicians.
Kahana, who is now a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, served in a short-lived non-Netanyahu government in 2021 and 2022 as minister for religious services in which he clashed with ultra-Orthodox Jews by seeking to reduce the power of the Chief Rabbinate.
Kahana himself is an observant Jew, part of Eisenkot's efforts to form a broad coalition that ranges from secular liberals to religious conservatives.
As parliament speaker, Kahana succeeds Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally who has held the position since 2022.
The parliament speaker serves as acting head of state when the president is unable to perform his duties.

Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government
The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu .
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot , the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu .
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.
He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.
The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.
They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.
Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.
Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.
Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

A US Army officer arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia earlier this month has been taken into US military custody, British counter-terror police have said.
The serviceman has been identified as Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, BBC News understands. The 41-year-old - who served in the US Army since 2008 - was arrested near Gloucester last week by British counter-terror police.
Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
Counter Terrorism Policing said he is now in US custody over suspected national security and espionage allegations. At the time of his arrest, Russia said it had "nothing to do with it".
British police previously said he was being held in London after he was arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023, which relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
The day after Tyner's arrest on 10 November, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he was "unaware" of what it was connected to.
"We have nothing to do with it, and it has nothing to do with us," he told reporters in Moscow.
The US serviceman is understood to have been based at Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire
On Tuesday, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them [their American partners] to progress."
"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," he added.
Tyner's arrest was the result of a long-running operation by MI5 - the UK's domestic intelligence and security agency - in collaboration with the FBI, the BBC understands.
He had previously served in Afghanistan and Iraq, but at the time of his arrest was working with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps near Gloucester - where he was said to be entrusted with sensitive information which would have been extremely damaging if leaked to Russia.
Detectives sent the Crown Prosecution Service a file on the senior US soldier's alleged spying for consideration - allegations described by the head of Counter Terrorism Policing as "extremely serious."
But at that stage the Attorney General's Office in London got involved. As did the US authorities.
And now the decision has been taken that Lieutenant Colonel Tyner should be taken into custody by the US Military.
It means he will not stand trial in the UK, but under US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
FBI director Kash Patel said an army officer was in custody "as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation" between the bureau, US Army and various UK partners.
"Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action," he said.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath" they all take.
"Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he added.

Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested by British police on 10 November over allegations related to espionage
A US soldier who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia has been taken into custody by the US military, police have said.
Lt Col Brandon Carroll Tyner, 41, was detained by British counter-terrorism police ‌on 10 November in Gloucestershire over allegations relating ⁠to espionage.
The arrest was part of an investigation by UK Counter Terrorism Policing, working with authorities including the US military and the FBI.
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said in a statement on Tuesday: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.
“That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase.
“An army officer is in custody as the result of an espionage investigation and the close cooperation between the FBI’s Philadelphia field office and Legat London and our partners at UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.
“Together we worked to identify a potential threat to national security and take swift action.”
The suspect, a senior soldier, was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire, which serves as the headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the Guardian understands.
He was arrested on suspicion of offences under section 1 and section 3 of the National Security Act and was in custody at a London police station.
US authorities have said Tyner joined the military in 2008 as a senior human resources officer, and was deployed overseas to Iraq, Qatar and Afghanistan.
He was identified on Friday after British counter-terror police secured more time to question him.
As part of the investigation, officers carried out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan police said last week.
Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing: said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS [Crown Prosecution Service], who in turn engaged with the attorney general’s office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.
“This decision was made in line with existing international protocols.
“These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.
“I’d like to praise the excellent work of the investigation team here in the UK to get us to this point and we will continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards.”
The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.
US Brig Gen Sean Stinchon said the case “should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the constitution”.
He added: “Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardising our collective defence, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served.
“This effort is a great example of the remarkable partnership Army Counterintelligence Command has with army prosecutors, the FBI, DOJ [Department of Justice], and the UK.”

BBC's Madeline Halpert explains why the US lost its measles elimination status and what it could mean.
After more than two decades, the US has lost its measles-free status, following two years of record case numbers and deaths.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a specialised service of the United Nations, determined the US has had uninterrupted transmission of the same strain of measles for more than 12 months.
Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, announced that Mexico and Bolivia have also lost their measles elimination status, attributing the resurgence in the region to persistent "gaps in vaccination".
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said it was committed to "regaining measles elimination status" by expanding access to vaccines.
The US has seen 5,400 cases of measles this year alone, with 10 measles-related deaths, the most the country has seen since the 1990s.
The measles virus - with its signature blotchy red rash - used to infect millions of children a year before a vaccine was invented. The extremely contagious virus can be fatal, and some patients can experience long-term complications including encephalitis and immune amnesia, which resets the immune system, leaving it with only limited ability to respond to new infections.
The US recommends two measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots for children between ages one and six, which is 97% effective in protecting against the illness.
PAHO, a group within the World Health Organization, revoked the US's measles-elimination after determining that the virus had circulated nonstop for more than a year.
"These figures are a serious warning for our region," PAHO's director Barbosa said at a news conference on Tuesday. "Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination."
He added that Canada, which lost its status of having eliminated measles last year after seeing several large outbreaks, has made strides this year to interrupt transmission.
Daniel Salas, the executive manager of immunisations at PAHO, said that the US and others who lost elimination status would be required to submit corrective action plans outlining how they would attempt to improve vaccination rates.
US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr Kennedy has attempted to make a series of sweeping changes to US vaccine recommendations and policies. The vaccine sceptic has also frequently cast doubt on the safety of MMR shot, as vaccination rates have declined across the US in recent years.
Kennedy has argued that the rise in measles cases started before he took the helm at HHS and that neighbouring countries have also seen more infections.
Responding to Tuesday's announcement, the CDC said the agency and its partners were "committed to stopping measles outbreaks, protecting Americans, and regaining measles elimination status".
"Together, we will encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection," the agency said.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the measles elimination designation was not what protected Americans.
"Vaccination does," she said. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities."
In a post on social media, Kennedy said: "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," he also said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."
The UK, Spain and Austria were among European nations that lost their measles-free status earlier this year, along with countries including Russia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan.
Nuwan Gunawardhana, an assistant professor of medicine with Columbia University Irving Medical Center, said the US losing its elimination status was "a huge leap backwards".
The US was the first country to eliminate measles in the Americas thanks to vaccination campaigns, noted William Moss, a paediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Dr Gunawardhana said it took massive efforts from public health officials and clinicians to build trust with patients to increase uptake of the MMR vaccine, leading to decades in the US with few infections and deaths.
But that trust has been steadily eroding since the Covid-19 pandemic, when Dr Gunawardhana said patients were confronted with misinformation about the safety of vaccines and lost even more trust in public health systems.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity, which limits the spread of measles and protects those who cannot get vaccinated, including newborns.
The vaccination rate for MMR across the US has fallen to 92.4%, below the 95% level that provides herd immunity - which limits the spread of measles
An outbreak in Pennsylvania has infected over 1,400 people - likely a large underestimate - and killed seven people, according to state officials.
Kennedy, the health secretary, has sparred with Pennsylvania officials over how it is counting the measles deaths, with CDC declining for now to record some of the deaths in its database.
Last year, the health secretary fired all the members of a top vaccine advisory panel and replaced them with his own appointees, some of whom were vaccine critics.
The panel recommended a number of vaccine changes - including no longer requiring the Hepatitis B vaccine for all newborns - but those recommendations were blocked by a federal judge.
President Donald Trump this year also cast doubt on the safety of the MMR vaccine, issuing an executive order for the shot to be split into three separate immunisations for measles, mumps and rubella, a move public health experts say is costly and could sow confusion about an already safe vaccine.
Doctors and public health officials say the misinformation from Kennedy and Trump has played a major role in falling vaccination rates.
"It's confusing patients. It's confusing families," Dr Gunawardhana said. "We need a clear message from the top."
The federal government's vaccine manoeuvres have left public health officials and states to fill in the gaps, offering their own separate recommendations upholding decades-long practices.

Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
The leaders of China , the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine .
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran .
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

Iran claims drone strike on US radar was retaliation for alleged airspace violations by US military drones.
Kuwait’s army has said the Gulf country is under attack by drones while the United States and Iran traded blows, marking escalating tensions in the region as a peace deal remains elusive.
The military said in a statement on X on Tuesday that “any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks”.
The US earlier carried out several attacks on Iran’s southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain.
“The American attack on locations on Qeshm island caused no damage to residential, commercial, or infrastructural areas,” Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency on Tuesday.
He said the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.
A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran’s earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.
US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain “were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel”.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it carried out a “precision operation” with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, in response to “repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones”.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.
It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days after a lull of several weeks. Friday’s strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported. Reuters said it came after a Bahraini court sentenced 64 people, mostly Shia clerics, to life in prison for allegedly colluding with Iran.
Kuwait’s armed forces said on Tuesday night that its air defences were responding to “hostile drone attacks” and urged the public to follow safety instructions.
It did not say where the drones came from or whether there were casualties or damage.
Iran’s armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday. The US military says it cleared the main routes of mines.
Since the war began on February 28, Iran has tried to restrict traffic through the strait , which normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, insisting that ships use only routes it has authorised. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers.
Another tanker, the Panamanian-flagged Tara Gas, was struck on Monday about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, causing a fire in its engine room, according to the security firm Vanguard.
Vanguard and India’s ports minister initially said all 25 crew, 24 of them Indian, were safe. But the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the vessel was hit a second time and the crew were “currently unaccounted for”. India’s ports minister later said the crew had abandoned the vessel after a second attack and that one Indian sailor was missing. Another Panamanian-flagged tanker, the On Phoenix, was hit by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast on Monday.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat, Oman’s news agencies said.
A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

El Salvador’s security minister has confirmed the troops will leave once kidnapped technicians are rescued.
Demonstrators have marched in several Haitian cities to show support for a deployment of troops from El Salvador, despite concerns that the outside intervention may worsen instability in the Caribbean country.
On Tuesday, hundreds of protesters rallied in the streets of cities like the capital, Port-au-Prince, bearing signs with slogans like “Down with the gangs”.
Haiti has long struggled with gang violence, but the crisis worsened around 2021, after the assassination of President Jovenel Moise. His death further weakened Haiti’s central government, and experts say gangs took advantage of the eroding public confidence to expand their influence.
The October 18 kidnapping of four Salvadoran aviation technicians near Port-au-Prince prompted El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele to respond with a military operation to Haiti.
But on Monday, El Salvador confirmed it would end its deployment of about 2,500 troops once the missing Salvadoran airmen were found.
“If they reappear tomorrow, as President Bukele said, we will leave,” Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said.
That announcement, however, was followed by public gestures of support and diplomatic engagements, with some top officials in Haiti encouraging the Salvadoran deployment to stay.
Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier travelled to San Salvador on Monday and expressed gratitude for the troop surge.
“The Haitian people applaud the decision of Nayib Bukele to send troops,” Pelissier said on Monday.
He added that Haitian security forces, together with their international counterparts, had recently managed to regain control of Haiti’s national football stadium, held by gangs for years.
“During the operation, we discovered several human skulls inside the stadium,” Bukele claimed in a social media post last week.
The timeline for the Salvadoran troop withdrawal is uncertain. While El Salvador has framed its deployment as a rescue mission, the leader of Haiti’s 400 Mawozo gang, Wilson Joseph, told The Associated Press that the four technicians are already dead.
Joseph added that the abduction took place in territory controlled by Chen Mechan, a rival gang. He provided no evidence to back his assertions.
Bukele, however, has championed his country’s role in confronting Haiti’s gangs, using social media to promote the offensive and sharing videos of military operations.
The Salvadoran president — who once referred to himself as the “world’s coolest dictator” — has been credited with popularising a “mano dura” or “strong hand” approach to regional security.
Faced with one of the highest homicide rates in the world, Bukele launched a hardline security crackdown on gangs in El Salvador in 2022, including mass arrests and mass trials.
His heavy-handed approach has led to a sharp decline in crime but has also been widely condemned for human rights abuses.
Critics have warned that transplanting such tactics to Haiti could spark a backlash, leading to greater instability and risks to civilians.
They have also criticised the lack of long-term planning for El Salvador’s troop deployment; a sudden withdrawal, for instance, could worsen the situation for Haiti’s security forces.
Bukele is campaigning for a third term in El Salvador’s February presidential election, and analysts speculate his actions in Haiti could be used as a campaign tool to drum up support.
The Salvadoran deployment is the latest in a series of international interventions in Haiti.
Such foreign involvement is often controversial. The United States, for instance, has sent troops to Haiti on multiple occasions in the 20th century, occupying the country for decades and seizing control of its central bank.
More recently, a United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) arrived in Haiti in April, to help address the widespread gang violence.
Gangs control more than 80 percent of the capital region. The conflict has killed more than 22,000 people since 2022. UN reports attribute more than half of the deaths in the first nine months of the year to security operations, including the deaths of 300 civilians.
The UN also says almost 2,000 people have been displaced since the arrival of Salvadoran troops.
But Pelissier said Haiti’s government had not reported any civilian casualties in the latest operations, which he described as professional.
“The best to do is to avoid, as much as possible, human rights violations, and that’s what we are doing together,” the minister said.

Indigenous Awá people of Amazon make contact with villagers and accept food to take back to territory
About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest , several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.
According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.
The village they entered was within the Arariboia Indigenous territory in the north-eastern state of Maranhão, home to the Guajajara ethnic group.
Local community leaders said the villagers offered food to the group.
“They asked for yams and took them back into their forest,” said Survival International.
The NGO explained that the Awá typically subsist on hunting and gathering. However, they have faced increased incursions from illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers.
A video of the encounter, filmed by Guajajara villagers and released by Survival International, shows a group of men, women and children at the edge of the forest.
Partially concealed by vegetation, they appear naked and are wearing necklaces. The men carry bows and long arrows.
“The physical condition of some members, particularly the children and the elderly, caused concern among the villagers, who noted clear signs of severe emaciation,” warned Coapima, an organization representing Indigenous groups in Maranhão.
Coapima highlighted the risks that unplanned contact poses to such groups, noting that they are particularly “exposed to diseases” against which they have little to no immunity.
Funai, the public agency responsible for Indigenous affairs, said in a statement sent to AFP that its technical teams were closely monitoring the situation and analyzing available information regarding the group’s health.
Survival International’s director, Caroline Pearce, said the group’s choice to emerge from isolation was a “troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger”.
She said the Awá were being driven into “an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction”.
According to the NGO, about 196 “uncontacted” peoples and groups, who choose to live in isolation, have been identified across 10 countries.
More than 90% of such groups live in the Amazon rainforest, primarily in Brazil , with others in Indonesia and India.
The Forest Guardians – a group of Guajajara people who have battled illegal invasions for years – warned in comments in the Survival International statement that “climate change, fires, deforestation and land encroachment” were affecting the Awá’s way of life.
According to Survival International, many of the guardians have lost their lives trying to protect the territory they share with the Awá.

Daithi O’Corrain, 48, has been charged with damaging a US military C-130 aircraft while it was parked overnight.
An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and damaged a United States military C-130 aircraft at an Irish airport, prosecutors have alleged.
Daithi O’Corrain, 48, was indicted by a grand jury in New York on Monday, with the indictment unsealed on Tuesday. Prosecutors claim that the Irish man left the plane “effectively destroyed”.
An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest at the US-Israel war on Iran and Washington’s support for Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza – a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians .
“An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide,” organiser Tracey Ryan wrote.
O’Corrain is expected to be “brought to and arrested in the Southern District of New York”, the indictment said. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of destruction of government property.
O’Corrain plotted the attack for months, US prosecutors said, searching online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel.
According to prosecutors, he then breached security at Shannon Airport on April 11 and barricaded himself inside the parked aircraft.
He allegedly cut wires and hydraulic lines and smashed every gauge in the cockpit.
O’Corrain also inflicted damage on the exterior of the aircraft with an axe, prosecutors said, and poured ball bearings into the transport plane’s fuel tanks.
“As a result of O’Corrain’s attack, the aircraft was effectively destroyed,” the office of the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.
“The damage inflicted rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the aircraft – worth approximately $60 million – will not return to active flight status.”
Shannon Airport, which was used by US President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a US military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a US military jet was parked.

Thousands of Haitians took to the streets on Tuesday to urge El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to keep fighting gangs, as his troops bolster security forces in the Caribbean nation. But experts warn that growing public support could turn to anger without a long-term plan to tackle violence and strengthen Haiti's police.
Thousands of people poured into the streets of Haiti ’s capital and beyond Tuesday to praise El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele and his troops as they fight gangs in the Caribbean nation.
“Keep fighting … because otherwise, they’ll end up killing us all,” one sign read.
“Give them the drones and the dogs!” others yelled in reference to the explosive drones that have targeted areas controlled by powerful gangs and the newly unveiled robot dogs making their rounds in Port-au-Prince.
By Tuesday night, Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier, who is in El Salvador , told reporters there was “no date” for the Salvadoran troops to leave, and that their support was necessary to reinforce Haitian police at least until elections are held next year. He said they would work on establishing a legal framework so Salvadoran forces can stay longer. Meanwhile, Haiti's government announced that the Council of Ministers ratified a cooperation deal between the two countries but did not provide specifics.
Read more Haitian police retake national stadium after two years of gang control
Last month, Bukele deployed some 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on October 18 and remain missing. Fighting between gangs and foreign forces backed by Haitian authorities has only increased since then as Haiti remains mired in violence, with more than 20,000 people killed in the past five years and gangs controlling an estimated 70% of Port-au-Prince.
“The gangs drove us out; they burned our houses and killed our children. They even killed pregnant women. We have lost everything,” he said. “We say thank you to our father, Bukele.”
Marie Michelle Dorville, a 55-year-old street vendor who joined Tuesday's march, said gangs killed her partner and left her with three children to raise.
“Bukele is an air of hope,” she said as she called on him and police to kill gangs “once and for all, so everyone can have a normal life.”
Sam Vigersky, a fellow with the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a report published Tuesday that Haitians cheering on Bukele is understandable: “El Salvador’s deployment of more troops in two weeks than the UN -backed mission did in over one year has generated a long-dormant sentiment among many Haitians: hope.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
By Tuesday afternoon, police fired tear gas and broke up the crowd as it headed to a stadium that Haitian and foreign forces recently secured. It had been in the hands of gangs for more than two years, preventing Haiti from playing its World Cup qualifiers at home.
While chants of “Bukele!” are spreading across Haiti, experts warn there’s no long-term plan to keep the country safe once the Central American troops pull out.
“This enthusiasm … could turn into anger against the government if the troops withdraw,” said Diego Da Rin, an analyst with International Crisis Group.
The group published a report Tuesday based on more than 100 interviews with officials in Haiti and abroad that reveal government failures and missteps as it urged Haitian officials to develop a plan to prevent their country from imploding once international forces leave.
“The new foreign mission promises temporary relief from the bane of gangs, but its goal is to weaken, not dismantle them,” the report said. “Haiti should start preparing now for the day when its own forces are once again summoned to take sole charge of the nation’s security.”
Forces currently fighting gangs include Haiti’s police and soldiers; a UN-backed gang suppression force; self-appointed vigilantes; and Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former US Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince. Fighting gangs largely on their own are some 2,500 Salvadoran troops deployed when four of their own went missing after they were attacked deep in gang-controlled territory.
International Crisis Group warned that authorities lack a strategy to identify threats, coordinate efforts and reduce violence long-term.
Echoing that sentiment was a recent cartoon in Le Nouvelliste newspaper that depicted Haitians cheering on Bukele as they stood near a table with a piece of paper on which someone had written “PLAN ANTI GANG” with crayons of various colours.
Tuesday’s report noted that plans to establish a National Security Council tasked with creating a long-term strategy to make Haiti safer two years ago never materialised.
Citing interviews with former senior government officials, the report stated that some people were concerned the council would oversee intelligence gathering, which has previously been used by Haitian leaders to target political opponents. Sources also told International Crisis Group that top officials did not want to see intelligence funds redirected because they feared losing that money.
International Crisis Group also said a foreign adviser said that a lack of national strategy means that various police units “often follow different operational guidelines depending on their foreign donors.”
As of last year, Haiti’s National Police had no more than 8,000 active officers for a country of nearly 12 million people, the report said, citing “sources with firsthand knowledge.” Many of those officers occupy command and administrative positions and are not on the street, “while others are not trained for combat.”
The report said the government shortened training from seven months to less than four to quickly increase the number of police officers.
It also warned that police promotions rarely follow criteria like seniority or merit, with some rank-and-file officers opting to work with gangs or turning to private security or arms trafficking for additional income. Lower-ranking officers in Haiti are paid about $300 a month before mandatory deductions.
International Crisis Group called for improving salaries, benefits and facilities for police officers, as well as offering them specialised training and a “clear promotion system based on performance rather than politics.”

The number of victims is expected to grow as foreign forces increasingly rely on helicopters and explosive drones – two things that Haitian security forces lack – to target gangs.
At least 87 civilians, including 21 children, were killed by drones from July 2025 to September 2026, according to the UN.
“Against this backdrop, the humanitarian indicators are moving in the wrong direction: 5.8 million Haitians facing acute hunger and 1.5 million displaced, both records,” Vigersky of the Council on Foreign Relations wrote.
In the first quarter of 2026, the number of civilians killed or injured by security forces as a fraction of all casualties rose 24%, according to the International Crisis Group, and that number is expected to increase.
International Crisis Group said the use of such weapons “has brought diminishing returns … producing no meaningful changes in territorial control” or a change in the balance of power on the ground.

Students oppose appearance of self-described ‘race realist’ who made plagiarism claims against Jason Arday
Hundreds of protesters filled the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford , to voice their opposition to an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”.
The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition from students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment.
Oriel, which allowed the Reform society to use a lecture theatre, declined to cancel the booking, saying it had a “statutory duty” to allow the blogger and academic to appear.
Earlier this year, Cofnas was the first to raise accusations of plagiarism against Prof Jason Arday .
Arday died weeks later, having resigned from his post as professor at the University of Cambridge, amid sustained media scrutiny which began with Cofnas’s claims .
The crowds outside sought to block the college’s main entrances, with hundreds chanting “Say his name – professor Jason Arday”, while several protesters held signs reading “Remember professor Jason Arday”.
One of the protesters, a first-year student studying English and German, who declined to give her name, said: “I think, given the situation at Cambridge with Jason Arday and given what happened, that we as an institution would be looking to not replicate that in any way or hinting that we could support that notion, [but] acting as an example in opposition.
“I think [Oxford and Cambridge], as two academic institutions, should be working together to banish this from ever happening again. And the fact that we can’t even act as the example, I think, makes me almost ashamed to be a part of this.”
Tommy, a second-year maths student at Oxford, said: “This is not the first of this kind of event. There was Tommy Robinson and the Oxford Union, and obviously there were protests for that as well. So I think it’s quite a nasty pattern that we’re seeing with these Oxford societies pandering to the far right, which is just really dangerous.”
Inside the lecture theatre, Cofnas was asked if he wanted to apologise to Arday’s family, but he declined. He said the implication behind the question was that “we shouldn’t criticise powerful figures”.
Cofnas added: “I would ask the people at Cambridge University who protected him for three years, who suppressed all criticism … I would ask them these questions,” earning a brief round of applause.
About 40 people made it into the venue, with less than a third of the space filled. Protests outside could be heard throughout Cofnas’s talk. At times some members of the audience appeared disengaged, looking at their phones.
Cofnas spent the majority of an hour talking about the history of what he called the “race equality thesis”, and his reasons for questioning it.
He has previously written that black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment” under a meritocratic system.
Anneliese Dodds, the MP for Oxford East, said she had contacted Oriel College after receiving complaints from constituents.
Dodds said: “Cofnas’ views are both repellent and contrary to the facts. Many of my student constituents have therefore contacted me to express their concerns about the student reform society choosing to provide him with publicity.
“I have written to Oriel College to ask what they are doing to act on students’ concerns about this meeting, including on safety grounds.”
While the protests were largely peaceful, a group of police appeared towards the end of the event to clear protesters from the entrances.
Hannah, a first-year law student, said that the size of the protest was proof that “even if Oxford won’t listen to us and won’t cancel the event, we’re still going to show up and we’re going to show that we won’t let that decision silence us. And we will still show that we don’t approve of this and we don’t want this type of behaviour here.”
Misan Harriman, the photographer and former chair of trustees of the Southbank Centre, said he attended the protest because he was concerned by the “damaging” rhetoric that Cofnas espoused.
“The university has failed all the students, not just the black students, by having them see this as something that could be remotely seen as part of the course of free speech,” Harriman said.

Actress Gabrielle Creevy stars as Liz Rich, bringing "absolute authenticity to the role"
The "real-life ghost story" of a family who experienced "frightening, inexplicable" things after moving to the countryside has been turned into a new TV drama.
The Witch Farm tells the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich who left London with their son Jonathan for a remote farmhouse in the foothills of the Brecon Beacons, determined to make a fresh start.
At first the isolation felt like freedom, but the family claimed things began to happen around the house leading them to feel increasingly scared.
Writer and creator, Danny Robins, met Liz who told him "her incredible story", becoming a four part series he beleives will "really surprise people".
Danny Robins hopes that new TV drama will raise the question, do ghosts exist?
Robins, who was also the executive producer of the project, explained how the idea for the four-part series came from a podcast he made for the BBC called The Battersea Poltergeist , which he described as being based on "another real-life ghost story".
"It was a hit around the world and afterwards there was a lot of pressure to find a sequel," he said, which led him to discover the story of Liz and Bill Rich.
In 1989, the young couple moved their family into a remote farmhouse at the foot of a mountain. They claimed to have experienced poltergeist activity, apparitions, alleged possessions and even physical injury.
They say this lasted for seven years and changed them forever, as well as affecting the community around them.
Robins said: "The more I dug into it, the more it felt like something that merited a long-form approach and so we made the podcast series called The Witch Farm .
"Through that process, I met Liz and she told me her incredible story. We also found other witnesses and pieced everything together through a mix of audio drama and documentary.
After finishing the podcast, Robins asked himself "what's next?", admitting that telling the story as a TV documentary "didn't feel right", leading to the decision to dramatise it instead.
The Witch Farm is based on the "truly nightmarish" tale of Liz and Bill Rich
Asked what he hopes viewers will feel when they watch the series, Robins said: "I absolutely want people to feel scared, but I also want them to be moved by it.
"It's an incredibly powerful and emotional story, that was one of the things that grabbed me when I first came across it for the podcast."
He also hopes that viewers will "laugh a little", adding that "humour has always been important" to his work.
Robins also hopes to raise the question – 'do ghosts exist?', sparking the debate between belief and scepticism.
"What's crucial for me is that I want viewers to think about it and reach their own conclusions," he said.
The upcoming drama, which was filmed in Wales, stars Port Talbot-born actress Gabrielle Creevy.
She said: "I'm from Wales and I love working here. It's always a pleasure and crews are always so great. I love working in the middle of nowhere in the fresh air - I think I'll always feel the same."
Robins said she brought "absolute authenticity to the role" through her Welsh accent."
Creevy recently featured in the new season of spy thriller Black Doves where she also uses her Welsh accent.
Robins said The Witch Farm is "such a Welsh story", which was considered throughout making the production.
He said an "almost entirely Welsh" crew was used in it's creation, adding: "It's been important that this feels like a story made and told in Wales."
The Witch Farm will be available on BBC iPlayer, BBC One and BBC One Wales from Sunday, 22 November.

Northern Ireland are in the Nations League top-flight after topping their group after a draw in Hungary; Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland's proud record of not having conceded in this campaign but Justin Devenny equalised
Justin Devenny's superb strike saw Northern Ireland earn promotion to the top tier of the Nations League with a hard-fought 1-1 draw away to closest challengers Hungary in Budapest.
Barnabas Varga ended Northern Ireland's proud record of not having conceded in this campaign when he fired the hosts in front after 35 minutes - a goal that also sent Hungary to the top of the group.
But moments after Isaac Price had hit the post for Michael O'Neill's young side, Devenny smashed the ball into the top left-hand corner in the 65th minute to restore Northern Ireland's one-point advantage as group leaders.
The visitors were on the back foot for much of the first half, with Hungary captain Dominik Szoboszlai hitting the post, but O'Neill, serving a touchline ban in the stands as former captain Steven Davis led things from the touchline, orchestrated key substitutions.
Northern Ireland started with Patrick Kelly in place of the suspended Jamie Donley up front but brought on Josh Magennis at half-time before Kieran Morrison and Brodie Spencer soon followed to help the visitors become a much greater threat going forward.
Magennis' physical presence and the extra pace paid dividends as, just two years after earning promotion from League C, Northern Ireland completed an unbeaten campaign in Group B2 to secure their place at the top table of European football.
Without Donley, the lack of a clear outlet told in a first half that saw Hungary come forward time and again.
There was a big panic after five minutes following an uncharacteristic mistake from Pierce Charles, whose pass went straight to Bendeguez Bolla, a late change to the Hungary side, who whipped in a superb low cross from which skipper Szoboszlai struck the post.
Northern Ireland were pegged back but might have snatched the lead from a Ciaron Brown long throw in the 33rd minute. However, Tom Atcheson did not seem to realise how much space he had as he prodded a weak shot towards his Blackburn team-mate Balazs Toth.
Two minutes later Pierce Charles launched a long free-kick into the box. Brown went down under an Andras Schafer challenge, but as Northern Ireland appealed in vain for a penalty, Toth kicked it long. Trai Hume got his head to the ball but could not get it as far as Pierce Charles, allowing Varga to nip in and score.
O'Neill will have felt the frustration of his ban with his side trailing at half-time, but his changes worked regardless.
Terry Devlin, the matchwinner on Saturday, had already fired into the side-netting before Price's low strike from the edge of the box cannoned back off the post.
Four minutes later they were level. Hume's long throw almost fell for Shea Charles but instead sat up for Devenny to take a touch before thumping an unstoppable strike into the top corner.
As time ticked down, Hungary pushed forward in increasing desperation - with Rajmund Toth firing over late on - but Northern Ireland dug in with the defensive resilience which has been the cornerstone of this campaign.
Northern Ireland boss Michael O'Neill speaking at his post-match press conference:
"It's a great feeling for us. We set out when we came into this level of the competition to first of all try and stay and we knew to be in the top two positions would help us.
"We knew that would help us potentially with the draw for Euro 2028 (qualification), but to come away unbeaten, to finish top, and to give the performance we've given against some very good teams, it's very encouraging.
"We had to dig really deep. We had to make substitutions; we had to try and get freshness. I felt in the first half we looked a little bit leggy, which is natural, but I just felt we needed that freshness at the right points in the game.
"But it was the belief we could get back into the game. We did that, and it was the belief that we could see the game out."
On Deveny's equaliser: "I was surrounded by Hungarian supporters, so I had to be slightly restrained! It was a celebration which was muted, shall we say!"

Ahmet Kural'ın Baki'siyle üç sezondur izleyicileri hem güldüren hem hüzünlendiren Gassal, final sezonuyla bu hafta geri dönüyor. Üstelik dijital platformlarda yoğun bir hafta var: Netflix 'in milyarlarca dolarlık FTX skandalını anlatan dizisinden Percy Jackson'ın yeni sezonuna kadar 7 yapım 17-23 Kasım arasında izleyiciyle buluşuyor.
'Ölünce beni kim yıkayacak?' sorusuyla yola çıkan Gassal'da merakla beklenen gün geldi. Ahmet Kural'ın başrolündeki dizinin dördüncü sezonu 19 Kasım Perşembe günü tabii'de yayına giriyor.
Platformun daha önce yaptığı açıklamaya göre bu sezon aynı zamanda dizinin finali olacak. Sümeyye Karaarslan'ın kaleminden çıkan yeni sezonda Baki'nin yalnızlığı, hayatına giren meraklı komşusu Gülşen ile daha da derinleşiyor. Gülşen'e Özlem Tokaslan hayat verirken kadroda Bülent Şakrak ve Deniz Cengiz de yer alıyor.
Fragmanda yalnızca bir anlığına görünen Hande Soral'ın Nihan'ının final sezonunda ne kadar yer alacağı ise hâlâ hayranların en çok merak ettiği konular arasında.
Haftanın bir diğer yerli yapımı romantik komedi türündeki Çiçekçi Kız. Deniz Akçay 'ın hem yaratıp hem yazıp hem de yönettiği dizide, kendi dükkânını açan genç bir çiçekçinin yolu gizli görevdeki bir polisle kesişiyor.
Helin Kandemir ile Hakan Çelebi'nin başrolleri paylaştığı dizinin kadrosunda Ayşen Gürler, Müge Su Şahin, Bayram Bazarov, Şebnem Yıldırım, Yusuf Demircioğlu, Yunus Narin ve Murat Karasu da var.
Netflix 'in haftadaki en çok konuşulacak yapımlarından biri, kripto dünyasını sarsan FTX çöküşünü ekrana taşıyan The Altruists. Sekiz bölümlük dizi , Sam Bankman-Fried ile Caroline Ellison'ın hikâyesini ve borsanın milyarlarca dolarlık dolandırıcılık skandalıyla nasıl çöktüğünü anlatıyor.
New York Magazine'de yayımlanan araştırma yazılarından uyarlanan diziyi The Imitation Game'in Oscar'lı senaristi Graham Moore ile Jacqueline Hoyt yarattı. Julia Garner ve Anthony Boyle'un yanı sıra Alex Lawther, Karan Soni, Madison Hu, Matt Rife ve Paul Reiser da kadroda.
Rick Riordan'ın sevilen serisinden uyarlanan Percy Jackson ve Olimposlular, üçüncü sezonuyla geri dönüyor. Yeni sezonda Annabeth'in kaçırılmasının ardından Percy, Thalia ve Artemis'in Avcıları'yla güçlerini birleştirerek hem arkadaşını kurtarmaya hem de Titan Kronos'un yeniden yükselişini durdurmaya çalışıyor.
Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries ve Aryan Simhadri'ye bu sezon Tamara Smart, Charlie Bushnell, Dafne Keen ve Kate McKinnon da eşlik ediyor.
Arjantin yapımı Gordon, Marcelo Larraquy'nin aynı adlı biyografik kitabından uyarlandı. Dizi , Aníbal Gordon'un hikâyesini anlatıyor: 1970'lerde küçük soygunlarla başlayan Gordon, suç örgütleri ve devlet güvenlik birimleriyle kurduğu ilişkiler sayesinde cinayetlere karışan güçlü bir figüre dönüşüyor.
Pablo Trapero ile Pablo Fendrik'in yönettiği dizide Rodrigo de la Serna'ya Kar Kardeşliği'nden tanıdığımız Matías Recalt eşlik ediyor.
Kasper Bajon'un yarattığı dizi , 1988'de dört çocuğun öldürülmesiyle ilgili soruşturmanın bir polisle bir psikiyatristin dostluğunu nasıl bitirdiğini anlatıyor. 25 yıl sonra hüküm giymiş bir katilin serbest kalma ihtimali ise ikiliyi geçmişte verdikleri kararlarla yüzleşmeye zorluyor.
Başrollerde Agnieszka Grochowska, Agnieszka Żulewska ve Michał Pawlik yer alıyor.
Haftayı kapatan yapım, aynı adlı Kore- Japonya ortak çizgi romanından uyarlanan suç gerilimi The Blue Road. Tokyo'da üzerinde Korece bir mesaj bulunan bir ceset bulunuyor, ardından Seul'de benzer bir cinayet işleniyor. Bunun üzerine iki ülkenin dedektifleri, sınır tanımayan bir seri katili yakalamak için birlikte çalışmak zorunda kalıyor.
Sekiz bölümlük dizinin başrollerinde Son Suk-ku, Eita Nagayama, Kim Shin-rok, Choi Sung-eun ve Jung Jae-young var.

Manuela Perteghella had criticised plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.
The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.
The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.
The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.
The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.
Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.
"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.
The planned move from Mason Croft has been paused while the university explores future options
The university said it would work with the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, institute staff, students, alumni and other partners over the coming months.
Tickell said the university's commitment to Shakespearean studies had "never been in doubt" but added that interest in studying in Stratford had remained low for several years.
He said related subjects had seen significant growth on the university's Birmingham campus, while the city's creative industries sector offered opportunities for Shakespearean research and scholarship.
"Over the next six months, we will work with the Shakespeare Institute, the RSC, the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, and other partners, students, and alumni to ensure that the Shakespeare Institute re-establishes itself at the heart of scholarship, performance and reception for England's greatest poet in both Birmingham and Stratford-upon-Avon," he added.
Earlier on Tuesday, Liberal Democrat MP Perteghella described the proposed move as "ill-thought" and "shocking".
She said she would raise the issue in Parliament and write to the university about her "deep disappointment" and concerns for the institute's future.
The University of Birmingham said it would spend the next six months exploring the centre's future
The MP backed a petition launched by the Stratford Herald calling on the university to keep the institute in Stratford-upon-Avon.
Actors Samuel West and Dame Janet Suzman have also backed the campaign.
The Shakespeare Institute, which celebrated its 75th anniversary in July, was founded at Mason Croft in 1951 and has worked with academics, writers and performers including Dame Judi Dench.
